quiz.q: What does a lifetime actually track?
options: How much memory a value uses
How long a reference stays valid (how long its target exists)
How many times a value is cloned
quiz.explain: A lifetime describes how long a reference is valid, so the compiler can forbid references that would outlive the data they point at.

quiz.q: Does adding a lifetime annotation like `'a` make data live longer?
options: Yes, it extends how long the value exists
No, it only describes a relationship the compiler then checks
Only for String, not for other types
quiz.explain: A lifetime annotation describes an existing relationship between references; it never allocates or prolongs anything.

quiz.q: When do you usually have to write an explicit lifetime like `'a`?
options: On every function that uses references
When a function returns a reference and takes more than one reference
quiz.explain: Rust's elision rules cover the common cases. You mainly need explicit lifetimes when a function returns a reference and takes multiple references, so Rust can't tell which the output borrows from.

quiz.q: Why does this fail to compile: a reference `r` set to `&value` inside a block, then used after the block ends?
options: value is dropped at the block's end, so r would dangle
You can't use & inside a block
r needs to be declared mut
quiz.explain: The value is dropped when its block ends, so r would point at freed memory. The compiler says 'value does not live long enough' and rejects it.

flashcards.back: Rust's tracking of how long a reference stays valid — how long the thing it points at is guaranteed to exist. Used to forbid dangling references.
No. A lifetime annotation only describes a relationship between references so the compiler can check it. It never allocates or prolongs anything.
